deep.reconstruction:
This page contains no mathematics: no formulas, no computations, no derivations. It is a continuous prose fragment in natural philosophy and epistemology. It is part of Riemann's notes printed by Weber and Dedekind in the Gesammelte Werke (1876, 'Fragmente philosophischen Inhalts', section 'Erkenntnisstheoretisches'). It continues the question from the previous page, 'I. Wann ist unsere Auffassung der Welt wahr?', whose answer is: when the connections among our representations correspond to the connections among things.

Argument on this page, restated:
(1) The elements of our picture ('Bild') of the world are totally different from the real elements they stand for. Only the connections ('Verbindungen') between elements must agree in picture and reality for the picture to be true. In modern terms this is a structure-preserving correspondence (a homomorphism or isomorphism of relational structure) between a model and its target. Nothing about the intrinsic nature of the elements needs to match.
(2) The truth of the picture does not depend on its fineness ('Feinheit'), i.e. on how large a portion of reality each element of the picture represents ('repräsentiren', 'vertreten').
(3) The connections must still correspond. In particular, the picture must not posit an immediate action between two elements where in reality only a mediated one occurs. Such a picture is false and needs correction. This prepares the action-by-contact principle stated on the next page: every distance-dependent action is propagated through space.
(4) Refinement is different from falsification. Suppose one element is replaced by a group of finer elements, so that its properties follow partly from simpler properties of the finer elements and partly from their connections. Then insight into the connection of things grows, but the earlier, coarser picture is not thereby declared false. In modern terms, refinement of a model, or coarse-graining, preserves truth at the coarser level.

Second question: 'II. Woraus soll der Zusammenhang der Dinge gefunden werden?' Answer: 'from the connection of the phenomena' (Erscheinungen). An inserted passage, marked as a supplement from another sheet, follows:
(a) What is given to deliberate reflection on nature is the representation of sense-objects in definite spatial and temporal relations.
(b) The qualities of sensible marks (colour, sound, tone, smell, taste, warmth or cold) are taken from our sensation alone and do not exist outside us. This is the classical primary/secondary quality distinction.
(c) Therefore the connection of things must be recognised from quantitative relations. These are the spatial and temporal relations of sense-objects and the intensity relations of the marks and of their qualitative differences.
(d) Knowledge of the connection of things must arise from reflection on the observed connection of these magnitude relations ('Grössenverhältnisse').

The next page applies this programme to reducing the general laws of inanimate nature to action through a continuous medium. All of the above restates the text; nothing is added by me except the modern glosses.
errors: No mathematical errors are possible because no calculation is present.

Philosophically, the claim that refinement never falsifies the coarser picture is asserted without argument. It holds only if the coarse connections are themselves preserved under refinement. The text implicitly assumes this, since point (3) excludes exactly the case where they are not.

results.what: Truth of a world-picture consists in the correspondence of connections (relations) between picture-elements and real elements, not in any similarity of the elements themselves.
results.modern_name: Picture theory of knowledge / structural correspondence, an early form of structural realism
results.usually_credited_to: Helmholtz (sign theory, 1860s-1878) and Hertz (Bildtheorie, Prinzipien der Mechanik, 1894); later Russell and Worrall (structural realism)

results.what: Truth is independent of the fineness of the picture; replacing an element by a group of finer elements increases insight without falsifying the earlier picture, whereas positing immediate action where reality has only mediated action makes the picture false.
results.modern_name: Model refinement / coarse-graining consistency; rejection of action at a distance

results.what: Sensible qualities (colour, sound, smell, taste, warmth) exist only in sensation; nature must therefore be known through quantitative spatial, temporal and intensity relations.
results.modern_name: Primary/secondary qualities distinction; quantitative programme of physics
results.usually_credited_to: Galileo (1623), Descartes, Locke (1690); Helmholtz's physiology of the senses

deep.surprise_reason: This is Riemann's well-known epistemological fragment, published in his Gesammelte Werke in 1876. It has been discussed repeatedly by historians (e.g. Scholz, Bottazzini, Ferreirós, Pulte), including as a forerunner of Hertz's Bildtheorie. It contains no mathematics, and its ideas are standard 19th-century natural philosophy.
transcription_corrections: The transcription matches the image closely and agrees with the printed Werke text.
In the image, 'unsere' (line 'so wächst dadurch unsere (die) Einsicht'), 'gegeben', 'Qualität' and 'quantitative' are underlined in the manuscript.

Marginal pencil folio number '(20)' circled at the right beside section II; ink page number '39' at top right; a faint pencil note at the bottom (roughly 'Li..f (5)') is not transcribed and is not clearly legible.
